claims.text: Superconducting properties in high-entropy alloys are governed primarily by the interplay of configurational disorder and electron count.
The interplay of configurational disorder and electron count modulates the local electronic density of states and phonon spectra.
Changes in the local density of states and phonon spectra alter electron-phonon coupling, which is critical for Cooper-pair formation.
The (TaNb)x(ZrHfTi)1−x family exhibits superconductivity at ambient pressure with measurable Tc and Hc2.
The proposed baseline alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase material.
The proposed baseline alloy exhibits conventional BCS, electron-phonon-mediated superconductivity.
High mixing entropy enforces a disordered but homogeneous atomic arrangement.
Atomic disorder alters the local electronic structure and phonon dynamics.
Changes in electron count adjust local electronic states.
Disorder-induced changes and electron-count-induced changes collectively determine Tc and Hc2.
Substantially different compositions in the (TaNb)1−x(ZrHfTi)x family can have similar ideal mixing entropies.
Replacing Zr with uranium can lower the effective electron count and reduce Tc and Hc2 relative to the Zr analogue while approximately retaining mixing entropy.
Increasing mixing entropy at constant electron count will subtly decrease Tc.
Increasing mixing entropy at constant electron count will suppress superconducting anisotropy.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to homogeneous, single-phase alloys with conventional electron-phonon-mediated superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism may not apply after phase separation, development of substantial nonequilibrium microstructure, or emergence of strong electronic correlations.
The individual quantitative contributions of electron count and configurational disorder are not yet well established.
Spin-orbit coupling may make a secondary contribution to the superconducting properties.
A lack of statistically meaningful changes in Tc or Hc2, or a lack of corresponding density-of-states or phonon-spectrum changes, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
